set1.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set1.q: Which three elements form the basic triad of descriptive epidemiology?
opts: Who, what and why
These are three of the five W's of epidemiology; the descriptive triad is person, place and time.
Incidence, prevalence and mortality
Incidence, prevalence and mortality measure disease burden; the descriptive triad is person, place and time.
Person, place and time
Correct: person, place and time are the essential characteristics of a descriptive study, understood before any analytic study is undertaken.
Host, agent and environment
Host, agent and environment are the triad assessed in analytic epidemiology; the descriptive triad is person, place and time.

set1.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set1.q: Researchers compare past exposures in people who have a disease with those in people who do not, to test whether the exposure causes the disease. Which branch of epidemiology is this?
opts: Analytic
Correct: relating an exposure to an outcome to test a cause-effect hypothesis is analytic epidemiology; the case-control study is one of its typical designs.
Descriptive
Descriptive epidemiology describes distribution by time, place and person; comparing exposures to test a cause is analytic.
Syndromic
Syndromic describes a surveillance system based on clinical features, not a branch of study; testing a cause-effect hypothesis is analytic.
Sentinel
Sentinel describes a surveillance system of prearranged reporters; comparing exposures between cases and non-cases is analytic epidemiology.

mis.Syndromic: surveillance type confused with study branch
mis.Sentinel: surveillance type confused with study branch

set1.io: 3 — Describe key events in the history and development of epidemiology, including genomic epidemiology
set1.q: What did the 1950 study by Doll and Hill link?
opts: Water supply and cholera
Water supply and cholera was John Snow's work in the mid-1800s; Doll and Hill linked smoking and lung cancer.
Diet and heart disease
Factors behind cardiovascular disease were the aim of the Framingham Heart Study; Doll and Hill linked smoking and lung cancer.
Lice and epidemic typhus
Doll and Hill studied a behavior, not an infection; their 1950 study linked smoking and lung cancer.
Smoking and lung cancer
Correct: Doll and Hill, 1950, linked smoking and lung cancer, an early application of epidemiology to behavior-related health outcomes.

mis.Lice and epidemic typhus: infectious example confused with behavioral study

set1.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set1.q: Which of Hill's criteria requires that exposure precede disease?
opts: Temporal sequence
Correct: temporal sequence requires that exposure precede disease; with a latency period, exposure must precede the latent period.
Biological gradient
Biological gradient is a dose-response relationship; exposure coming before disease is temporal sequence.
Consistency
Consistency is the same finding across studies, populations and designs; exposure preceding disease is temporal sequence.
Specificity
Specificity is an exposure leading to a single or characteristic effect; exposure preceding disease is temporal sequence.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 46 and 50

set1.io: 2 — Describe the specific uses for epidemiology training
set1.q: Evaluating vaccine and clinical trials, and managing the staff and resources they need, belongs to which use of epidemiological training?
opts: Program evaluation and management
Correct: program evaluation and management covers evaluating prevention and intervention programs, such as vaccine and clinical trials, and managing their staff and resources.
Outbreak response
Outbreak response is identifying, reporting and investigating outbreaks in a timely way, not running and evaluating trials.
Training and mentoring
Training and mentoring health professionals is a separate use; evaluating and managing vaccine and clinical trials is program evaluation and management.
Public health communication
Communication is developing and delivering public health messages; evaluating and managing trials is program evaluation and management.

set1.io: 6 — Define reportable disease
set1.q: Where is cancer reported?
opts: It is not reportable
Cancer is reportable: it is one of the groups, reported to state cancer registries, and it appears on the notifiable list.
To state cancer registries
Correct: cancer is reported to state cancer registries, its own group among the reportable conditions.
By telephone to the state
Telephone reports are required for rubeola and pertussis; cancer goes to state cancer registries.
As a yearly total of cases
Reporting totals applies to chickenpox and influenza; cancer is reported to state cancer registries.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 22 and 23

set1.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set1.q: Which type of epidemic is often zoonotic or vector-borne?
opts: Other
Correct: the category 'other' covers epidemics that are often zoonotic or vector-borne, such as Lyme disease and West Nile encephalitis.
Propagated
Propagated epidemics are person-to-person; zoonotic and vector-borne epidemics fall under 'other'.
Common source, point
A point source is a brief shared exposure such as one meal; zoonotic and vector-borne epidemics are 'other'.
Mixed
Mixed epidemics begin from a common source and then propagate person to person; zoonotic or vector-borne ones are 'other'.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 55 and image on Slide 58

set1.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set1.q: A county counts residents newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes during the past year and divides by the county's residents at midyear. What is it measuring?
opts: Prevalence
Prevalence would count all residents who have diabetes, new and old; counting only the newly diagnosed measures incidence.
Cause-specific mortality
Cause-specific mortality counts deaths from a specific cause; this counts new diagnoses, which is incidence.
Case fatality rate
The case fatality rate is deaths over total cases; new diagnoses over the population is incidence.
Incidence
Correct: new cases arising during a given period, over the population, is incidence; the numerator of incidence is new cases only.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 27 and 28

set1.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set1.q: Morbidity in a population is measured by which two measures?
opts: Basic and effective reproduction
Reproduction numbers describe how many cases one case generates; morbidity is measured by incidence and prevalence.
Incidence and prevalence
Correct: morbidity is measured by incidence (new cases over a period) and prevalence (all cases present over a period).
Crude and infant mortality
These are mortality rates, measuring deaths; morbidity is measured by incidence and prevalence.
Sensitivity and specificity
These are critical characteristics of surveillance; morbidity is measured by incidence and prevalence.

set1.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set1.q: Which measure was part of the population approach to youth smoking?
opts: Higher taxes on tobacco
Correct: the measures included eliminating tobacco smoke in public places, decreasing advertising and promotion, decreasing youth access to tobacco and increasing taxes on tobacco.
Lower taxes on tobacco
Taxes on tobacco were increased, not lowered, as part of the population approach.
More tobacco advertising
Advertising and promotion of tobacco were decreased, not increased, alongside higher tobacco taxes.
Easier youth access to tobacco
Youth access to tobacco was decreased, not made easier, alongside higher taxes and less advertising.

set1.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set1.q: Besides vaccination, what else adds to herd immunity?
opts: Lowering the case fatality rate
The case fatality rate is deaths over cases; herd immunity grows with natural immunity after recovery as well as vaccination.
Recovery from the infection
Correct: herd immunity is often discussed with vaccination, and it is also impacted by natural immunity gained by recovery from the infection.
Treating cases with antibiotics
Treatment is not named as a source of immunity; herd immunity is impacted by natural immunity gained by recovering from the infection, as well as by vaccination.
Reporting cases to authorities
Reporting monitors disease and warns of outbreaks but immunizes no one; natural immunity after recovery adds to herd immunity.

set1.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set1.q: What is the prevailing wisdom in epidemiology about judgments of cause and effect?
opts: One strong study settles them
One study is not enough to fix a judgment; most are tentative, consistency across studies matters, and new evidence can change them.
They rest on association alone
Causation is inferred from association and other factors, such as Hill's criteria; and judgments stay tentative.
They are tentative and open to new evidence
Correct: most judgments of cause and effect are tentative and are open to change with new evidence.
They are final once a study is published
Publication does not settle them; most judgments of cause and effect are tentative and open to change with new evidence.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 43 and 53

set1.io: 3 — Describe key events in the history and development of epidemiology, including genomic epidemiology
set1.q: What is genomic epidemiology?
opts: Mapping cases by home and workplace
Mapping where cases lived and worked is a spot map, descriptive epidemiology; genomic epidemiology monitors pathogens' genetic makeup.
Monitoring the genetic makeup of pathogens
Correct: genomic epidemiology is the process of monitoring the genetic makeup of the pathogens that cause disease, made possible by advances in sequencing.
Tracing inherited disease in families
Genomic epidemiology studies the pathogens' genes, not inherited human disease; it monitors the genetic makeup of disease-causing pathogens.
Testing new vaccines in clinical trials
Evaluating vaccine and clinical trials is program evaluation; genomic epidemiology monitors the genetic makeup of pathogens.

mis.Tracing inherited disease in families: human genetics confused with pathogen genomics

set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 12 and 69

set1.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set1.q: In the person-place-time triad, which of these is a 'person' characteristic?
opts: Climate and humidity
Climate effects such as temperature and humidity are 'place' characteristics, not person ones.
Urban or rural setting
Urban, suburban or rural setting is a 'place' characteristic; socioeconomic status is a person characteristic.
Seasonal pattern
Seasonal variation is a 'time' characteristic; person characteristics include socioeconomic status.
Socioeconomic status
Correct: person characteristics include age, gender, socioeconomic status (education, occupation, income), marital status, ethnicity or genetic profile, and behavior.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 34, 35 and 36

set1.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set1.q: Which mortality rate is used to compare health status between countries?
opts: Infant mortality rate
Correct: the infant mortality rate, the number of infant deaths, is used to compare health status between countries.
Crude mortality rate
The crude mortality rate counts deaths from all causes in a population; the rate used to compare countries' health status is infant mortality.
Cause-specific mortality rate
A cause-specific rate counts deaths from one cause; comparing countries' health status uses infant mortality.
Case fatality rate
The case fatality rate is deaths over cases of a disease; comparing countries uses the infant mortality rate.

set1.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set1.q: Where does case surveillance begin?
opts: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention receives notifiable cases after local and state health departments collect them; the process begins locally.
Hospital billing offices
Billing is not part of case surveillance; it begins with local and state public health departments collecting data on cases.
Community health surveys
Surveys collect data from individual persons; case surveillance begins with local and state health departments collecting data about cases.
Local and state health departments

Correct: case surveillance begins with local and state public health departments collecting data about cases; notifiable conditions are then reported on to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

set1.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set1.q: A relative risk that is either very high or very low is less likely to be due to chance or bias. Which of Hill's criteria is this?
opts: Consistency of findings
Consistency is the same result across multiple studies and populations; a very high or very low relative risk is strength.
Biological gradient
Biological gradient is a trend in relative risk across doses; a single very high or very low relative risk is strength of association.
Temporal sequence
Temporal sequence is exposure preceding disease; a very high or very low relative risk is strength of association.
Strength of association
Correct: a strong association is one in which the relative risk is either very high or very low, and it is less likely to be caused by chance or bias.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 46 and 48

set1.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set1.q: A surveillance system counts cases of diarrhea rather than laboratory-confirmed cholera. Which type of surveillance is this?
opts: Active surveillance
Active surveillance is defined by staff contacting providers; using clinical features alone for the case definition is syndromic.
Genomic surveillance
Genomic methods identify pathogens by their genetic makeup, the opposite of a clinical-feature definition; this is syndromic surveillance.
Syndromic surveillance
Correct: syndromic surveillance uses case definitions based entirely on clinical features, such as diarrhea instead of cholera; it is the system most often found in developing countries.
Sentinel surveillance
Sentinel surveillance is defined by a prearranged group of reporters, not by clinical case definitions; counting diarrhea instead of cholera is syndromic.

set1.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set1.q: What is the first step in investigating a communicable disease outbreak?
opts: Develop a focused hypothesis
A focused hypothesis comes after cases are defined and described with descriptive epidemiology.
Implement control measures
Control and prevention measures come near the end, after the hypothesis is evaluated and refined.
Establish its existence
Correct: the investigation begins by establishing the existence of an outbreak, then preparing for field work and verifying the diagnosis.
Verify the diagnosis
Verifying the diagnosis comes third, after establishing the outbreak and preparing for field work.

set1.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set1.q: In John Snow's analytic study, houses supplied by the company that drew its water from where had far more cholera deaths?
opts: The Thames upstream of London
Upstream water was the protective source: the Lambeth Company moved its intake upstream of London, and its houses had a far lower death rate.
A deep brewery well
The brewery's deep well protected its workers in the descriptive study; the analytic comparison was between companies drawing from the Thames.
Rainwater cisterns
Cisterns were not part of the comparison; Snow compared houses supplied by the two companies drawing from the Thames, upstream versus downstream.
The Thames downstream of London

Correct: Snow's hypothesis was that water from below London carried cholera; houses supplied by the Southwark and Vauxhall Company, still drawing downstream, had a far higher death rate than Lambeth houses.

mis.A deep brewery well: adjacent fact from the descriptive study

set1.io: 4 — Identify common sources of epidemiologic data
set1.q: Air-quality ratings collected by sensors are which source of epidemiologic data?
opts: Nonhealth-related sources
Nonhealth-related sources are financial and legal records; air-quality sensor data are environmental.
The environment
Correct: the environment supplies data through samples and sensors for environmental changes, including air-quality ratings.
Individual persons
Individual persons are surveyed or given questionnaires; sensor readings of air quality are environmental data.
Health care providers
Providers notify the health department of cases of certain diseases; air-quality ratings come from the environment.

set1.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set1.q: Which term describes a disease that occurs at irregular intervals or as isolated incidents?
opts: Endemic
Endemic diseases are found at chronically low levels, a steady presence; isolated, irregular cases are sporadic.
Epidemic
An epidemic is an excess of cases over what is expected; isolated incidents are sporadic.
Pandemic
A pandemic is a worldwide epidemic; isolated, irregular incidents are sporadic.
Sporadic
Correct: sporadic diseases occur at irregular intervals or as isolated incidents.

set1.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set1.q: Which critical characteristic of surveillance allows individual persons with disease to be identified for treatment or quarantine?
opts: Timeliness
Timeliness lets control measures be implemented effectively; identifying individual persons with disease is sensitivity.
Representation
Representation gives an accurate picture of the disease's temporal trend; identifying individual cases is sensitivity.
Sensitivity
Correct: sensitivity allows identification of individual persons with disease, to facilitate treatment, quarantine or other control measures.
Specificity
Specificity excludes persons who do not have the disease; finding the persons who do have it is sensitivity.

set1.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set1.q: A study compares illness among residents living near a hazardous waste disposal site with residents living elsewhere. Which application of epidemiology is this?
opts: Social and behavioral epidemiology
Social epidemiology studies factors such as poverty and discrimination; a waste-site exposure is environmental epidemiology.
Policy development
Policy development uses evidence to shape policy; studying a waste-site exposure is environmental epidemiology.
Environmental epidemiology
Correct: environmental epidemiology studies how environmental factors affect health, including exposure to air and water pollution or to hazardous waste disposal sites.
Occupational health
Occupational epidemiology studies workers and their workplace conditions; residents near a waste site are an environmental exposure.

set1.io: 2 — Describe the specific uses for epidemiology training
set1.q: An epidemiologist describes who gets a disease, who dies from it and what its outcome is, to rank it against other diseases of concern. Which use of epidemiological training is this?
opts: Disease prioritization
Correct: disease prioritization evaluates and ranks diseases of concern, including describing the clinical picture: who gets the disease, who dies and what the outcome is.
Outbreak response
Outbreak response identifies, reports and investigates outbreaks in a timely way; ranking diseases by who gets them and who dies is prioritization.
Public health communication
Communication is developing and delivering public health messages; describing and ranking diseases of concern is disease prioritization.
Experimental epidemiology
Experimental epidemiology designs an experimental model to test a hypothesis; ranking diseases by their clinical picture is disease prioritization.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 7 and 8

set1.io: 2 — Describe the specific uses for epidemiology training
set1.q: Taken from its Greek roots, epidemiology is the science of what?
opts: What grows in the laboratory
Nothing in the roots refers to the laboratory; epi (upon) plus demos (people) plus ology (science) gives the science of what falls upon people.
What falls upon people
Correct: epi means upon, demos means people and ology means science, so epidemiology is the science that deals with what falls upon people.
What lives inside people
The roots are epi (upon) and demos (people), not a word for inside; epidemiology is the science of what falls upon people.
What spreads between animals
Demos means people, not animals; epidemiology is the science of what falls upon people, bridging biomedical, social and behavioral sciences.

set1.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set1.q: Why did the health department's response to the first Legionnaires' disease cases in 1976 start late?
opts: The department was closed for the weekend
Correct: doctors with the first cases tried to contact the state health department, but it was closed for the weekend, and by Monday 18 deaths had occurred.
The disease was not yet reportable
Reportability was not the problem described; the doctors tried to reach the department, but it was closed for the weekend.
Doctors refused to report the cases
The opposite: doctors with the first cases attempted to contact the health department, which was closed for the weekend.
The cases were outside the country
The convention was in Philadelphia; the delay came from the health department being closed for the weekend.

set1.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set1.q: Which type of surveillance uses staff members to contact health care providers regularly for data?
opts: Syndromic surveillance
Syndromic surveillance is defined by case definitions based on clinical features alone; staff contacting providers is active surveillance.
Sentinel surveillance
Sentinel surveillance relies on a prearranged group that agrees to report all cases; staff phoning providers regularly is active surveillance.
Active surveillance
Correct: active surveillance uses staff to regularly contact providers; it is the most accurate but the most expensive, and often used during outbreaks or seasonal events.
Passive surveillance
Passive surveillance waits for reports submitted by facilities and providers; regularly contacting providers is active surveillance.
set1.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 19 and 20

set1.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set1.q: In public health, interventions are most often designed on the basis of what?
opts: Genomic sequences
Sequencing helps link outbreak cases; public health interventions are most often designed on associations.
Associations
Correct: most often, in public health, interventions are designed on the basis of associations; causation is inferred, not usually proven first.
Proven causes
Waiting for proof of causation is not the usual practice; interventions are most often designed on associations.
Single case reports
A single case does not establish a population relationship; interventions are designed on associations.

mis.Proven causes: belief that causation must be proven first

set1.io: 6 — Define reportable disease
set1.q: What makes a disease reportable (notifiable)?
opts: It is usually fatal
Severity is one reason a disease is of public interest, but the definition is that reporting is required by law.
Law requires its reporting
Correct: a reportable (notifiable) disease is one required by law to be reported to government authorities.
It is caused by a bacterium
Reportable diseases include viral, parasitic and noninfectious conditions such as lead poisoning; the defining feature is the legal requirement to report.
It has no available treatment
Treatability does not decide it; a disease is reportable when the law requires reporting it to government authorities.

set2.io: 3 — Describe key events in the history and development of epidemiology, including genomic epidemiology
set2.q: Which 17th-century figure pioneered tabulating population health and mortality as rates, ratios and proportions?
opts: William Farr
William Farr worked in the 1800s, building on such counts to analyze Britain's mortality statistics; the 17th-century pioneer of tabulation was John Graunt.
Hippocrates
Hippocrates, around 400 BC, explained disease through environmental and host factors; tabulating mortality as rates came with John Graunt.
Doll and Hill
Doll and Hill linked smoking and lung cancer in 1950; the 17th-century pioneer of mortality tables was John Graunt.
John Graunt

Correct: John Graunt pioneered tabulating population health and mortality in rates, ratios and proportions, noting male-female differences, high infant mortality, urban-rural differences and seasonal variation.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 10 and 11

set2.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set2.q: Which three phenomena are assessed in analytic epidemiology?
opts: Exposure, latency and outcome
Latency belongs to the temporal-sequence criterion for causation; the analytic triad is host, agent and environment.
Host, agent and environment
Correct: the basic triad of analytic epidemiology is host, agent and environment.
Person, place and time
Person, place and time are the triad of descriptive epidemiology, understood first; analytic epidemiology assesses host, agent and environment.
Sensitivity, specificity and timeliness
These are critical characteristics of surveillance; analytic epidemiology assesses host, agent and environment.

set2.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set2.q: A survey asks every adult in a town whether they currently have asthma, and those answering yes are divided by the town's adults. What is it measuring?
opts: Prevalence
Correct: all cases present at or during a time period, over the population, is prevalence; a survey of who currently has a condition measures it.
Incidence
Incidence counts only new cases arising in a period; asking who currently has asthma counts all cases present, which is prevalence.
Crude mortality
Crude mortality counts deaths from all causes; current cases over the population is prevalence.
Attack rate
An attack rate is the proportion of an exposed group falling ill in an outbreak; current cases in a survey is prevalence.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 27 and 28

set2.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set2.q: Which critical characteristic of surveillance gives an accurate picture of a disease's temporal trend?
opts: Sensitivity
Sensitivity identifies individual persons with disease; the accurate temporal picture comes from representation.
Specificity
Specificity excludes persons without disease; the accurate temporal picture comes from representation.
Representation
Correct: representation is needed to provide an accurate picture of the temporal trend of the disease.
Timeliness
Timeliness is about implementing effective control measures; an accurate picture of the temporal trend needs representation.

set2.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set2.q: For a chronic disease such as osteoarthritis, which has a long duration and an onset date that is hard to pinpoint, which measure is usually used?
opts: Case fatality rate
The case fatality rate measures deaths among cases; for chronic disease burden with vague onset, prevalence is used.
Attack rate
An attack rate describes the ill among the exposed in an outbreak; chronic diseases with vague onset are measured by prevalence.
Prevalence
Correct: prevalence rather than incidence is often measured for chronic diseases such as diabetes or osteoarthritis, which have long duration and hard-to-pinpoint onset.
Incidence
Incidence needs the onset of each new case to be dated; for long chronic diseases with vague onset, prevalence is measured instead.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the specific uses for epidemiology training
set2.q: Epidemiology influences clinical medicine through its emphasis on what?
opts: Disease classification and diagnosis
Correct: epidemiology impacts clinical medicine because of its emphasis on disease classification and diagnosis.
Disease prevention
The emphasis on disease prevention is why epidemiology impacts public health; for clinical medicine it is classification and diagnosis.
Basic biological mechanisms
Understanding basic biological mechanisms is the link to pathophysiology; clinical medicine draws on classification and diagnosis.
Quantifying disease frequency
Quantifying disease frequency and its relationship to antecedents is the link to biostatistics, not clinical medicine.

set2.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set2.q: What does causation imply that an association alone does not?
opts: A statistical link between the two
A statistical relationship is what an association already is; causation adds a true mechanism from exposure to disease.
An exposure that is common
How common an exposure is does not make it causal; causation implies a true mechanism leading to disease.
A disease that is reportable
Reportability is a legal requirement; causation implies a true mechanism from exposure to disease.
A true causal mechanism
Correct: causation implies a true mechanism leading from exposure to disease; finding an association does not make it causal.

set2.io: 3 — Describe key events in the history and development of epidemiology, including genomic epidemiology
set2.q: Who is called the father of modern vital statistics?
opts: William Farr
Correct: William Farr systematically collected and analyzed Britain's mortality statistics in the 1800s, developed life-table approaches and reported his findings to authorities and the public.
John Snow
John Snow is called the father of field epidemiology, for his work on the London cholera epidemic; Farr is the father of modern vital statistics.
John Graunt
John Graunt pioneered tabulating mortality as rates and ratios in the 17th century; the father of modern vital statistics is William Farr.
Hippocrates
Hippocrates explained disease rationally through environmental and host factors; modern vital statistics began with William Farr.

set2.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set2.q: When communicating the findings of an outbreak investigation, which of these must be decided?
opts: Whether to repeat the study
Repeating the study is not one of the listed decisions; communication decides who needs to know, how and why.
Who needs to know
Correct: communicating findings means determining who needs to know, how the information will be communicated and why it needs to be communicated.
Who caused the outbreak
Assigning blame is not part of communicating findings; the steps are deciding who needs to know, how and why.
Which drug each case gets
Treatment of individual cases is not part of this step; communicating findings means deciding who needs to know, how and why.

mis.Which drug each case gets: clinical step confused with public health step

set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, image on Slide 68

set2.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set2.q: In describing disease over time, what is a secular trend?
opts: A rise and fall within each year
A pattern that repeats within the year is a seasonal trend; a secular trend runs over a prolonged period, usually years.
A single localized, stationary source
A localized and stationary source describes a point source; a secular trend is occurrence over years.
Spread from one person to the next
Spreading infection reflects a propagated pattern; a secular trend is disease occurrence over a prolonged period, usually years.
Occurrence over many years
Correct: a secular trend is the occurrence of disease over a prolonged period, usually years.

set2.io: 4 — Identify common sources of epidemiologic data
set2.q: During a foodborne illness outbreak, investigators hand questionnaires to people who ate at an event. Which source of epidemiologic data is this?
opts: Health care providers
Providers supply notifications to the health department when they see certain diseases; questionnaires gather data from individual persons.
The environment
Environmental data come from samples such as river water or soil and from sensors; a questionnaire collects from individual persons.
Nonhealth-related sources
Nonhealth-related sources are financial and legal records such as sales or court records; questionnaires collect from individual persons.
Individual persons
Correct: questionnaires and surveys collect data from individual persons, as in a foodborne illness outbreak or a national nutrition survey.

set2.io: 6 — Define reportable disease
set2.q: In the United States, notifiable disease data are collected through which system?
opts: The Framingham Heart Study
Framingham is a multigenerational study of cardiovascular disease, not a reporting system; notifiable data go through the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System.
National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
This national survey collects health data on United States residents from individual persons; notifiable disease data go through the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System.
National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System
Correct: in the United States, collection is done through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System.
State cancer registries alone
State cancer registries receive cancer reports; notifiable diseases as a whole are collected through the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System.

set2.io: 3 — Describe key events in the history and development of epidemiology, including genomic epidemiology
set2.q: In the 1960s and 1970s, epidemiological methods were applied to which worldwide achievement?
opts: Ending influenza outbreaks
Influenza keeps changing and remains a concern; the worldwide eradication achieved with epidemiological methods was smallpox.
Eradicating smallpox
Correct: in the 1960s and 1970s, epidemiological methods were applied to eradicate smallpox worldwide.
Eradicating cholera
Cholera was the subject of John Snow's 19th-century work; the worldwide eradication achieved in the 1960s and 1970s was of smallpox.
Eliminating tuberculosis
Tuberculosis remains a concern, including drug-resistant strains; the 1960s-1970s eradication was of smallpox.

mis.Eradicating cholera: adjacent disease from the same history

set2.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set2.q: What are exposures associated with a difference in disease risk often called?
opts: Indicators
An indicator is a measurable factor estimating the size of a health problem; exposures linked to disease risk are risk factors.
Vehicles
A vehicle is an environmental mode of communication bringing host and agent together; exposures linked to risk are risk factors.
Confounders
A confounded association is one level of the pyramid of associations; exposures associated with disease risk are called risk factors.
Risk factors
Correct: exposures associated with a difference in disease risk are often called risk factors.

set2.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set2.q: Which term describes a disease found at chronically low levels in a population?
opts: Pandemic
A pandemic is a worldwide epidemic; a chronically low level in a population is endemic.
Endemic
Correct: endemic diseases are found at chronically low levels in a population, evenly distributed rather than clustered.
Sporadic
Sporadic diseases occur at irregular intervals or as isolated incidents; a steady low level is endemic.
Epidemic
An epidemic is an excess over what is expected, or uncontrolled spread; a chronically low level is endemic.

set2.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set2.q: In the host-agent-environment triad, which of these is a host factor?
opts: Crowded housing
Living conditions such as crowding belong to the environment, not the host.
A biting vector
A vector is one of the environment's modes of communication that bring host and agent together.
A dietary allergen
Allergens are listed among the agents (environmental agents); immunologic status is a host factor.
Immunologic status
Correct: host factors are genetic endowment, immunologic status, personal characteristics, personal behavior, and definitive versus intermediate host in vector-borne disease.
set2.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 38, 39 and 40

set2.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
set2.q: When epidemiology is applied to a noncommunicable disease, what is the first step?
opts: Assess external validity
Assessing whether results apply to other populations is the last step; the first is defining the population of interest.
Define the population of interest
Correct: the steps begin by defining the population of interest, then creating measures of exposure and health indicators, sampling, estimating associations and evaluating causality.
Take a sample of the population
Sampling comes after defining the population and creating measures of exposures and health indicators.
Estimate measures of association
Estimating associations comes after the population is defined, measures created and a sample taken.

set2.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set2.q: Public health surveillance systematically collects, analyzes and interprets data for which purpose?
opts: Billing health insurers
Billing is not the purpose; surveillance collects and interprets data to facilitate the prevention and control of disease.
Proving disease causation
Surveillance measures what is happening and the effect of interventions; inferring causation is the work of analytic studies.
Preventing and controlling disease
Correct: surveillance systematically collects, analyzes and interprets data to facilitate the prevention and control of disease, and informs decisions about health.
Diagnosing individual patients
Surveillance looks at what is going on in the population; diagnosing one patient is clinical work. Its purpose is prevention and control.

set2.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set2.alt: A bar chart of measles cases by day of onset from mid-October 1970 to mid-January 1971: scattered single cases, then a cluster in mid-November, a taller peak in early December and the tallest peak in mid-December, each wave following the last.
set2.slide: Epidemic curve: measles cases by day of onset.
set2.q: This epidemic curve shows measles cases by day of onset, with a series of successively larger waves. Which type of epidemic does it show?
opts: Common source, continuous
A continuous common source gives cases spread over the period of exposure that stop when it is removed; successive growing waves show person-to-person spread.
Other, vector-borne
Vector-borne epidemics such as West Nile or Lyme fall under 'other'; measles waves building on each other show propagated spread.
Propagated
Correct: successive, growing waves of cases are the pattern of person-to-person (propagated) transmission, a spreading infection that may be extended.
Common source, point
A point source gives one sharp peak within a single incubation period; repeated, growing waves show propagated spread.

set2.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set2.q: A new therapy keeps people with an incurable disease alive far longer, while the number of new cases each year stays the same. What happens to the disease's prevalence?
opts: It falls
Prevalence would fall with a rapidly fatal course or rapid recovery; longer survival without cure raises it.
It stays the same
Incidence is unchanged, but prevalence also depends on duration; longer survival without cure raises prevalence.
It equals incidence
Prevalence counts all cases present and incidence only new ones; with longer survival prevalence rises further above incidence.
It rises
Correct: prevalence depends on incidence and duration; prolonged survival without cure lengthens duration, so prevalence rises even with unchanged incidence.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the specific uses for epidemiology training
set2.q: Epidemiology is described as a bridge between which fields?
opts: Law, economics and politics
Politics shapes policy, but the bridge epidemiology forms is between the biomedical, social and behavioral sciences.
Biomedical, social, behavioral
Correct: epidemiology bridges the biomedical, social and behavioral sciences, studying what falls upon people.
Surgery, pharmacy and nursing
These are clinical professions, not the fields named; epidemiology is a bridge between the biomedical, social and behavioral sciences.
Chemistry, physics and engineering
The physical sciences are not the fields it links; epidemiology bridges biomedical, social and behavioral sciences.

mis.Chemistry, physics and engineering: physical sciences confused with population science
mis.Law, economics and politics: policy influences confused with the bridged sciences

set2.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
set2.q: When planning public health surveillance, what must be identified first?
opts: A vaccine against the disease
No vaccine is needed to begin surveillance; what must come first is a clear objective that includes how data will be collected and analyzed.
A treatment for every case
Treatment is not a prerequisite; planning starts with a clear objective covering how the data will be collected, consolidated and analyzed.
A clear, stated objective
Correct: you must be able to identify a clear objective for the surveillance, including how the data will be collected, consolidated and analyzed.
A proven cause of the disease
Surveillance does not require a proven cause; it starts with a clear objective, including how data will be collected and analyzed.

set2.io: 6 — Define reportable disease
set2.q: Which notifiable disease is reported by telephone rather than in writing?
opts: Influenza
Influenza is reported as a total number of cases, with chickenpox; pertussis is reported by telephone.
Pertussis
Correct: rubeola and pertussis are in the group requiring a mandatory report by telephone.
Gonorrhea
Gonorrhea is in the mandatory written report group with salmonellosis; pertussis and rubeola are reported by telephone.
Salmonellosis
Salmonellosis needs a mandatory written report; the telephone group is rubeola and pertussis.

set2.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set2.q: How was the bacterium behind the 1976 Legionnaires' disease epidemic finally found?
opts: Testing of specimens thought dead
Correct: in December 1976, a laboratorian at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention located the source bacteria by continuing to test specimens that were thought to be dead.
A doctor isolated it on the first weekend
Nothing was isolated that weekend, when the health department was closed; the bacterium was found months later by persistent testing of specimens thought dead.
A survey of residents identified it
Surveys identify exposures, not organisms; the bacterium was found by a laboratorian who kept testing specimens thought to be dead.
Genomic sequencing matched the cases
Genomic epidemiology came much later; the bacterium was found by persistent laboratory testing of specimens thought to be dead.

mis.A survey of residents identified it: descriptive tool confused with laboratory method

set2.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
set2.q: How is the case fatality rate calculated?
opts: Deaths divided by total cases
Correct: the case fatality rate is deaths divided by total cases of the disease.
Deaths divided by the population
Deaths over the whole population is a mortality rate; the case fatality rate divides deaths by total cases.
New cases divided by the population
New cases over the population is incidence; the case fatality rate divides deaths by total cases.
Existing cases divided by the population
All cases present over the population is prevalence; the case fatality rate divides deaths by total cases.

set2.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
set2.alt: A bar chart of hepatitis A cases by date of onset in November and December: one food handler case marked as the presumed index case in early November, then a single tall, sharp cluster of cases in late November with a smooth curve over it, and a few secondary cases afterward.
set2.slide: Epidemic curve: hepatitis A cases by date of onset.
set2.q: This epidemic curve shows hepatitis A cases after one food handler fell ill, rising to a single sharp peak. Which type of epidemic does it show?
opts: Propagated
Propagated spread builds in successive waves from person to person; one sharp peak after a single source is a point common source.
Other, zoonotic
Zoonotic and vector-borne epidemics fall under 'other'; a single sharp peak traced to one food handler is a point common source.
Common source, point
Correct: the cases share one source and the exposure was brief, so they cluster into one sharp peak within about one incubation period: a point common source.
Common source, continuous
A continuous common source keeps exposing people over a longer time, giving a long, flat spread of cases; one sharp peak means a brief, point exposure.

set2.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set2.q: Findings repeated in multiple studies, across different populations, circumstances and study designs, satisfy which of Hill's criteria?
opts: Biological gradient
Biological gradient is a dose-response trend; agreement across studies, populations and designs is consistency.
Consistency of findings
Correct: consistency of findings is a result demonstrated in multiple studies, across different populations, in differing circumstances and with different study designs.
Strength of association
Strength is a very high or very low relative risk in a study; repetition across studies and populations is consistency.
Specificity of association
Specificity is an exposure leading to a single or characteristic effect; repetition across studies is consistency.

set2.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set2.q: In 1994, what change in approach to youth smoking did the Surgeon General's report recommend?
opts: Treat it as a community and population issue
Correct: the report recommended moving from campaigns focused on individual young people to addressing youth smoking as a community and population issue.
Focus campaigns on individual young people
That was the approach being replaced; the report recommended treating youth smoking as a community and population issue.
Leave the issue to individual families
The report moved away from individual-level focus toward a community and population approach.
Concentrate efforts on adult smokers
Adult smoking had already fallen by the 1980s; the report addressed youth smoking as a community and population issue.

set2.io: 10 — Compare and contrast applications of epidemiology, including policy development, outbreak investigation, social and behavioral issues, the environment and occupational health
set2.q: Policy development rests on values, ideology, politics and evidence. Which of these is epidemiology's main contribution?
opts: Evidence
Correct: evidence is the main contribution of epidemiology to policy; it is not usually the main influence on policy, but it is worth fighting for.
Values
Values are one basis of policy development, but epidemiology's main contribution is evidence.
Ideology
Ideology shapes policy too, but what epidemiology contributes is evidence.
Politics
Politics is one basis of policy development; epidemiology's main contribution is evidence.

set2.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
set2.q: Three studies each find that lung cancer mortality rises steadily from fewer than 10 to more than 40 cigarettes a day. Which of Hill's criteria does this rising trend most directly support?
opts: Biological gradient
Correct: a trend in risk with increasing dose, here more cigarettes per day, is a dose-response relationship, the biological gradient.
Specificity
Specificity is an exposure leading to a single or characteristic effect; a risk that climbs with dose is the biological gradient.
Temporal sequence
Temporal sequence asks whether exposure came first; a risk rising with each step in dose is the biological gradient.
Plausibility
Plausibility asks whether the mechanism makes biological sense; a stepwise rise with dose is the biological gradient.
